Une armée dont on se sert … — In Ernst Jünger’s translation:
“An army that is used for oppression must first itself be subdued. The hammer must endure as many blows as the anvil.”
E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke 14, Stuttgart 1978, p. 273.
Gerhard Nebel’s essay — In G. Nebel, Von den Elementen. Essays, Wuppertal 1947, pp. 9–31. The date of composition is given there as 1940, not “1941.”
“O happiness of the gnat” — See Rilke, Eighth Duino Elegy.
Ebeling’s thesis — See Gerhard Ebeling, Kirchengeschichte als Geschichte der Auslegung der Heiligen Schrift, Tübingen 1947.
Ils ont outragé l’esprit — “They have insulted the spirit.” The sentence comes from the French version of Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews, chapter 10, verse 29.

“If the fundamental proposition of evolution is true—namely that the whole world, animate and inanimate, is the result of the mutual interaction, according to definite laws, of the forces possessed by the molecules from which the primordial nebula of the universe was composed—then it is no less certain that the present world existed potentially in that cosmic vapor, and that an intelligence sufficient to know the properties of the molecules of that vapor could, for example, have predicted the state of the fauna of Great Britain in 1868 with as much certainty as one can say what will happen to the vapor of one’s breath on a cold winter’s day.”
Schmitt quotes Huxley through Bergson: Henri Bergson, L’évolution créatrice (Bibliothèque de philosophie contemporaine), Paris 1913, pp. 41–42.
the office of G. & K. — The office of the Graewe & Kaiser company in Plettenberg-Eiringhausen, where Schmitt’s father worked as an accountant.
“Even the most sublime ideas …” — Probably modeled on:
“The most civilized peoples are as close to barbarism as the most highly polished iron is to rust.”
In Ernst Jünger’s German translation: “The most civilized peoples are no farther removed from barbarism than the brightest iron is from rust.”
E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke 14, Stuttgart 1978, p. 257.
“Philosophy, being the fruit of long meditation and the result of an entire life, cannot and should never be presented to the people, who are always at the beginning of life.”
In Ernst Jünger’s translation: “Philosophy, as the late-ripened fruit of the mind and the autumn of life, must not be offered to the people, who always remain in childhood.”
E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke 14, Stuttgart 1978, p. 257.
Saint-Martin — Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin (1743–1803), mystical and theosophical writer and translator of Jakob Böhme into French.
κατέχων — The Katéchon, “the restrainer,” appears both in a personal form (κατέχων) and in a neuter form (κατέχον).
καὶ νῦν τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε, εἰς τὸ ἀποκαλυφθῆναι αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ καιρῷ. τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας· μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται.
“And you know what still holds him back, until he is revealed at his appointed time. For the mystery of evil is already at work; only the one who now holds it back must first be removed.”
In medieval theology, the “mystery of evil” was interpreted as the Antichrist, who appears at the end of time in the Book of Revelation.
The Katéchon was a central theme for Schmitt, and not only in his later years. On 20 October 1974 he wrote to Hans Blumenberg:
“For more than forty years I have been collecting material on the problem of katécwn, or katécon (Thess. 2:2, 6).”
See BW Blumenberg, p. 120, with notes on pp. 122–123.
In fact, Schmitt’s interest probably went back even further, to the middle of the 1920s, and was likely encouraged by Erik Peterson.
The material Schmitt collected on the subject survives among his papers, RW 265, nos. 20022, 20023, 20024, 20026, 20172, and 21149.
On the Katéchon, see also Nomos, pp. 28 ff.

Schmitt rejected the translation “one who delays” or simply “restrainer” when discussing the term with Sander and Julien Freund. See Carl Schmitt/Hans-Dietrich Sander, Werkstatt-Discorsi. Briefwechsel 1967–1981, edited by Erik Lehnert and Günter Maschke, Schnellroda 2008, p. 65, note 15:
“the word ‘Katechon’ does not mean to delay; it means rather ‘to hold down.’”

On 24 January 1980 Walter Warnach wrote to Herbert Nette about Schmitt’s understanding of the Katéchon. From a final conversation with Schmitt the previous autumn, Warnach understood that Schmitt’s concern was
“to protect Christianity from every suspicion of eschatologism and, accordingly, to anchor the medieval Empire and its mission in the world as firmly as possible in Scripture.”
Nette papers, Deutsches Literaturarchiv Marbach, HS 948460.

Adso — (c. 920–992), Benedictine abbot and author of a work on the Antichrist: Adso of Montier-en-Der, De ortu et tempore Antichristi, in Corpus Christianorum. Continuatio Mediaevalis 45, Turnhout 1976.

Haimo of Halberstadt (Migne X. 117, col. 779) — Haimo of Halberstadt, died 853, bishop. The commentary on Revelation to which Schmitt refers, printed in J. P. Migne’s Patrologia Latina, is now attributed instead to the Benedictine monk Haimo of Auxerre.

“Delusion, everywhere delusion” — From Hans Sachs’s monologue on delusion in Richard Wagner’s Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg. See Carl Schmitt, “Richard Wagner und eine neue ‘Lehre vom Wahn’,” in Bayreuther Blätter. Deutsche Zeitschrift im Geiste Richard Wagners 35, 1912, pp. 239–241.
Mrs. Winckelmann — Freda Winckelmann, wife of Johannes Winckelmann.

Père dom Deschamps — Léger-Marie Deschamps (1716–1774), Benedictine. His work Le Vrai Système ou le Mot de l’énigme métaphysique et morale, discovered only in 1862, made him appear as a precursor of Hegel.
Claude-Nicolas Ledoux — (1736–1806), French architect and one of the leading representatives of Revolutionary architecture.
Laberthonnière — Lucien Laberthonnière (1860–1932), Catholic theologian. See 6 December 1949.
Erich Voegelin — Eric Voegelin (1901–1985), political scientist and philosopher.

In connection with Graetz’s remark, Schmitt is referring to E. Voegelin, Rasse und Staat, Tübingen 1933; and in connection with the reference to Goethe, to E. Voegelin, Die Rassenidee in der Geistesgeschichte von Ray bis Carus, Berlin 1933. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 25790.
See also Schmitt’s correspondence with Voegelin in Schmittiana NF II, 2014, pp. 183–199.
Schubert — Gotthilf Heinrich von Schubert (1780–1860), natural scientist and philosopher of nature.
“Prometheus work” — No source can be identified; possibly an unrealized project by Nebel.
“So meaning, the more it searches for itself …” — Final stanza of the poem “Klage über der Schöpfung” by Konrad Weiß; Weiß, pp. 407–408.
Gilles — Werner Gilles (1894–1961), painter and friend of Carl and Duška Schmitt. For a time he lived in the Schmitt household at Kaiserswerther Str. 17 in Berlin.
Wehberg — Hans Wehberg (1885–1962), pacifist scholar of international law and author of a commentary on the Covenant of the League of Nations, first published in 1921.

Hegel — G. F. W. Hegel, Über die wissenschaftlichen Behandlungsarten des Naturrechts, seine Stelle in der praktischen Philosophie, und sein Verhältnis zu den positiven Rechtswissenschaften, in Jenaer kritische Schriften (II), newly edited by Hans Brockard and Hartmut Buchner, Hamburg 1983, pp. 90–178.
Also Hegel, “Hamanns Schriften,” in Sämtliche Werke, vol. XI: Berliner Schriften, Hamburg 1956, pp. 221–294.
Bilfinger — Carl Bilfinger (1887–1958), jurist. Thirty-eight letters and eight postcards survive among Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 nos. 1346–1393 and 18598.
Mentimur regnare Iovem … — This and the following quotations are from Pharsalia VII, 442 ff. Schmitt substituted “Germania” for “Arabes Medique Eoaque.”

Felices Arabes Medique Eoaque tellus, Quam sub perpetuis tenuerunt fata tyrannis. Ex populis qui regna ferunt sors ultima nostra est, Quos servire pudet. Sunt nobis nulla profecto Numina: cum caeco rapiantur saecula casu, Mentimur regnare Jovem.

“Happy are the Arabs and Medes, happy the East, whom fate has kept permanently under the rule of tyrants! Of all peoples forced to endure tyranny, ours is truly the worst fate, because we are ashamed to be slaves. No, for us there are no gods. Since the ages are swept along by blind chance, we lie when we say that Jupiter rules.”
Quod fugiens civile nefas redituraque numquam Libertas ultra Tigrim Rhenumque recessit.
“… freedom, fleeing the horrors of civil war and never to return, withdrew beyond the Rhine and the Tigris.”
Bella pares superis facient civilia divos —
Mortalia nulli Sunt curate deo. Cladis tamen huius habemus Vindicatam, quantam terris dare numina fas est: Bella pares superis facient civilia divos.
“No god cares for the fate of mortals. Yet the gods have paid the penalty for this disaster, as far as gods can make amends to men: civil war will make the deified dead equal to the gods above.”
H. Bung — Hubertus Bung (1908–1981), jurist and pupil of Schmitt.
Confusion with my namesake in Tübingen — Carlo Schmid.
The first letter from Herbert Lemmel—see above, note to p. 4—to Schmitt reached him in 1948 on a Russian postcard addressed to:
“Professor Carl Schmidt, French Zone, Tübingen am Neckar (Württemberg).”

It was therefore delivered in Tübingen to Württemberg councillor of state and professor Karl Schmid, who at that time had not yet begun calling himself “Carlo.” Schmid forwarded it to Plettenberg with a covering letter on stationery headed “Staatsrat Prof. Dr. Karl Schmid,” RW 265 no. 8725/2:
I assume that the writer of the enclosed letter was trying to reach you rather than me, and I am therefore sending his letter on to you.
